items.title: DACIA Maroc lance la DACIA Tour : un rendez-vous B2B dédié aux professionnels
items.description: Dacia Maroc a donné le coup d’envoi du Dacia Tour, une série de rencontres dédiée aux professionnels et décideurs du Royaume. Ce nouveau rendez-vous a proposé un temps d’échange autour des enjeux de développement des entreprises avec des experts et des besoins en matière de mobilité. Pour les professionnels, la mobilité est avant tout un choix rationnel. L’approche de Dacia repose sur quatre principes : la maîtrise des coûts, la simplicité, la tranquillité d’esprit et une gamme cohérente, afin de répondre aux besoins des entreprises. Programmé à Casablanca, Tanger, Agadir et Marrakech, cette sérié d’événements sera l’occasion pour Dacia Maroc de présenter son écosystème de solutions : véhicules, , présence industrielle, fiabilité, financement, réseau et services. Une rencontre autour des enjeux de croissance et de solution de mobilité pour les professionnels La rencontre de Casablanca s’est ouvrte par une plénière business autour de la thématique « Faire grandir son entreprise : quels sont les leviers de croissance ? ». Modérée par Hicham Bennani, cette plénière a réuni plusieurs intervenants et experts, dont Adil Raïs, président de la commission de croissance des TPME et Entrepreneuriat à la CGEM, Mohcine Benjelloun Directeur Général du CRI de Rabat, Omar boubakraoui, Directeur de la Transformation et de la croissance des entreprises MAROC PME et Fouzi Dinari Expert Commissaire aux comptes et conseils en entrepreneuriat, afin d’apporter différents éclairages sur les enjeux auxquels sont confrontées les entreprises. Un panel consacré à « Dacia, la solution pour votre mobilité professionnelle » a permis ensuite de présenter les réponses de la marque aux besoins des entreprises et des professionnels. Au-delà des prises de parole, le Dacia Tour a accordé également une place importante aux rencontres entre participants et aux solutions d’accompagnements professionnelles proposées par la marque Dacia. Des temps dédiés ont permis aux décideurs et entrepreneurs de prolonger les discussions, de partager leurs expériences et de développer de nouvelles connexions professionnelles. Avec cette initiative, Dacia Maroc affirme sa proximité avec les acteurs économiques et sa volonté de les accompagner dans leurs enjeux de mobilité. Le DACIA Tour à la rencontre des professionnels au Maroc Après Casablanca, le Dacia Tour se déplacera à Tanger le 17 novembre, à Agadir le 10 décembre, puis à Marrakech le 17 décembre. Dans chaque ville, l’ambition du Dacia Tour reste la même et réunira les professionnels de chaque région sur les mêmes thématiques : autour de temps d’échange consacrés aux enjeux des entreprises et aux solutions de mobilité. The post DACIA Maroc lance la DACIA Tour : un rendez-vous B2B dédié aux professionnels appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Treat all persons with dignity during interrogation – Mahama charges BNI
items.description: President John Mahama has stressed the need for the Bureau of National Intelligence (BNI) to protect the dignity and rights of persons brought in for interrogation. He says the newly renovated interrogation rooms of the BNI must provide a comfortable environment for persons who come into contact with the Bureau while ensuring that their dignity is respected. Speaking at the commissioning of the renovated interrogation centre, a new forensic laboratory and the presentation of 111 operational vehicles to the BNI, President Mahama said Ghanaians should ideally not have to find themselves in interrogation rooms, but those who do must be treated with dignity. “I pray that Ghanaians do not have to come to these interrogation rooms. But when they do, their dignity must be protected,” he said. The president disclosed that the interrogation rooms have been upgraded with soundproofing and digital recording equipment to improve the conduct and documentation of interrogations. He also talked about the importance of the newly established forensic laboratory in strengthening the Bureau’s capacity to investigate cybercrime and other sophisticated digital offences. “So, it is important that we have this forensic lab to check cybercrime and all the other sophisticated digital crimes that are being committed today,” he stated.

items.title: Nalerigu High Court bars five NDC members from regional elections
items.description: The High Court in Nalerigu has restrained five individuals, including disputed co-opted members of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in the Nalerigu-Gambaga Constituency, from participating in the party’s Regional Executive Elections scheduled for Saturday, November 14, 2026. The ruling follows escalating internal disagreements over the selection and legitimacy of five additional members co-opted into the constituency executive committee, exposing deep divisions within the party and an increasingly bitter contest for political influence in the constituency. Presided over by Justice Samuel Bright Acquah, the court granted an ex parte application filed by Safianu Akunloya Akukua and six others against the NDC and seven other defendants. The plaintiffs were represented by lawyer Issaka Balima Musah. The dispute, which has generated competing press conferences, accusations of constitutional violations and threats of legal action, is increasingly being viewed against the backdrop of a broader political rivalry between North East Regional Minister Ibrahim Tia and former Nalerigu-Gambaga MP and former Minister for Climate Change and Sustainability, Alhaji Baba Seidu Issifu. How the disagreement started The immediate disagreement centres on the selection of five additional constituency executive members and whether the process complied with the NDC Constitution. On November 10, 2026, the Constituency Chairman and some executive members held a press conference challenging the legitimacy of a proposed list of five co-opted members. They accused party officials of disregarding the authority of the constituency executive committee and facilitating the inclusion of individuals whose selection, they argued, had not followed the appropriate constitutional procedures. The group maintained that the process undermined internal party democracy and threatened to demonstrate and pursue legal action if the disputed list was not withdrawn. Their concerns also centred on the alleged involvement of the North East Regional Minister, Ibrahim Tia, in the process. Vice Chairman leads counterattack However, the constituency’s Vice Chairman, Abdulai Tahiru Yampasia, led a counter-press conference on Wednesday, November 11, alongside Deputy Secretary Ibrahim Basigi and 14 other executives. In a statement titled “ Setting the Record Straight: The Facts Behind the Co-option of Five Constituency Executive Committee Members ,” the group rejected the chairman’s allegations and defended the process as constitutionally legitimate. They alleged that the chairman and eight other executives walked out of a meeting convened on October 29 to deliberate on the co-option process. According to them, the Vice Chairman subsequently presided over the meeting, allowing the remaining 15 members of the 24-member constituency executive committee to continue deliberations. The 15 executives argued that they constituted a quorum under Article 50 of the NDC Constitution and unanimously agreed on the five-member list following consultations with the Regional Executive Committee. They also disputed the chairman’s position on the geographical distribution of the five positions. While the chairman’s side reportedly favoured three representatives from Gbintri and two from Sakogu, the 15 executives said their proposed arrangement was to allocate two positions each to Sakogu and Gbintri, with the remaining position going to Nagboo. They cited Articles 16(1)(r), 50 and 51 of the party’s constitution to justify the process. The group further rejected allegations of political interference by the Regional Minister, arguing that the Regional Secretary’s involvement was consistent with his responsibility to coordinate party activities. The two press conferences exposed a deep division within the constituency executive, with both sides insisting they were defending the NDC Constitution and the interests of the party. The bigger political battle: Ibrahim Tia versus Baba Issifu Beyond the constitutional arguments, JoyNews has monitored that the unfolding dispute is increasingly being viewed against the backdrop of an intense political struggle for influence and control of the Nalerigu-Gambaga Constituency between North East Regional Minister Ibrahim Tia and former MP and former Minister for Climate Change and Sustainability, Alhaji Baba Seidu Issifu. The rivalry between the two influential political figures has become a defining feature of the constituency’s internal political dynamics, with competing loyalties and interests increasingly reflected in disagreements among party executives. Tensions have remained high between supporters and sympathisers of the two political heavyweights, with previous disagreements spilling into public confrontations and, at one point, violence. In April this year, tensions within the NDC in the Nalerigu-Gambaga Constituency escalated into violence, leaving one man injured following an alleged mob attack linked to internal party disagreements. The victim, identified as Adam Shamuna, sustained an eye injury after he was reportedly assaulted by about 15 individuals believed to be affiliated with the East Mamprusi Municipal Chief Executive. The incident reportedly followed a heated exchange on an NDC WhatsApp platform over the distribution of fertiliser. In an interview with JoyNews, Shamuna alleged that his attackers were sympathisers of the current MCE and the North East Regional Minister, Ibrahim Tia. In June, another controversy over which of the two political figures was responsible for facilitating the rehabilitation of dams in Langbinsi and Nalerigu triggered further exchanges between their respective supporters. The rivalry also played out during the party’s recent internal elections, with both camps reportedly endorsing and financing candidates for various constituency executive positions. The outcome reflected a divided balance of power. Candidates reportedly backed by Ibrahim Tia won the positions of Vice Chairman, Organiser, Zongo Caucus Coordinator, Women’s Organiser and Deputy Women’s Organiser. On the other hand, candidates aligned with Alhaji Baba Issifu secured the positions of Chairman, Communications Officer, Youth Organiser and Deputy Regional Organiser. The results highlighted the extent to which the two political camps have entrenched their influence within the constituency’s party structures. The current disagreement between the constituency chairman and his vice chairman is therefore increasingly being interpreted within this broader contest for political control. The controversy over the five co-opted positions has assumed significance beyond the question of who qualifies to participate in the regional elections. The composition of the constituency executive committee determines, in part, the political influence, organisational authority and mobilisation structures available to competing factions within the party. Control of these structures could have significant implications for future party decisions, particularly the contest for the NDC parliamentary nomination ahead of the 2028 general elections. Although neither Ibrahim Tia nor Alhaji Baba Issifu is named as a defendant in the court proceedings, the political competition between their respective camps provides important context for understanding the intensity of the disagreement. Court intervenes ahead of Saturday’s elections In its November 12 ruling, the High Court said it had identified a triable issue concerning the alleged violation of the party’s constitutional provisions. Justice Samuel Bright Acquah indicated that judicial intervention was necessary to prevent further tensions and protect the integrity of the electoral process. “The court thinks it is necessary to intervene to forestall peace within the party… The court therefore grants the Motion Ex Parte, restraining 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th Defendants from participating in the Regional Executive Elections scheduled on the 14th of November, 2026.” The plaintiffs had argued that allowing the disputed individuals to participate in the elections would cause irreparable damage to their democratic rights and undermine the legitimacy of the electoral process. The order was issued under the hand and seal of the High Court in Nalerigu on November 12, 2026, and signed by Registrar Mohammed Muaweya.

items.title: IShowSpeed sacré streamer de l’année pour la troisième fois consécutive
items.description: Le créateur de contenu américain IShowSpeed continue de marquer l’univers du streaming. Il a remporté, jeudi 12 novembre 2026, le trophée de « Streamer of the Year » aux Streamer Awards 2026, pour la troisième année consécutive. Une distinction qui vient consacrer une année particulièrement riche pour celui qui avait notamment fait escale au Sénégal en janvier dernier, lors de sa tournée africaine. IShowSpeed confirme son hégémonie dans l’univers du streaming. Le jeune créateur de contenu américain a remporté, pour la troisième fois consécutive, le prix de « Streamer of the Year » lors de la sixième édition des Streamer Awards, organisée le 12 novembre 2026 à Los Angeles, aux États-Unis. Il avait déjà décroché cette distinction en 2024 et en 2025. Au-delà de ce sacre, le vidéaste est également reparti avec le trophée de « Best IRL Streamer », qui récompense les créateurs spécialisés dans les diffusions en direct de leurs expériences et interactions dans la vie réelle. Il a aussi été distingué dans la catégorie « Best Streamed Series » pour sa série consacrée à la Coupe du monde de football 2026. Au total, trois récompenses sont venues couronner sa soirée. Lire aussi: Le Sénégal en live (par Arame NDIAYE) Mais c'est surtout son discours de remerciement qui a retenu l'attention. À la surprise générale, IShowSpeed a choisi de s'exprimer entièrement en indonésien, adressant un clin d'œil à une communauté qui lui a réservé un accueil particulièrement chaleureux lors de ses précédents voyages. « Merci beaucoup à tous. Je suis parti de zéro, juste un petit garçon avec un grand rêve. Vous êtes avec moi depuis le début, vous n'êtes pas seulement des fans, vous êtes ma famille », a-t-il déclaré, selon la publication de Rapunchline. Un passage remarqué au Sénégal Cette nouvelle distinction fait également écho à son passage au Sénégal, en janvier 2026. Dans le cadre de sa tournée africaine baptisée « Speed Does Africa », le streamer avait posé ses valises à Dakar les 20 et 21 janvier, avec l'ambition de parcourir une vingtaine de pays en 28 jours. Une aventure suivie en direct par des millions d'internautes à travers le monde. Son séjour sénégalais avait été marqué par une immersion dans plusieurs facettes du patrimoine national. Première étape : l'île de Gorée. Vêtu du maillot de l'équipe nationale du Sénégal floqué du numéro 7, le jeune Américain avait découvert la Maison des Esclaves et son histoire. Une séquence particulièrement suivie par sa communauté internationale, au cours de laquelle il avait évoqué le lien historique entre l'Afrique et la diaspora afro-américaine. À Dakar, IShowSpeed avait également fait escale à la plage de Soumbédioune. Accueilli par les lutteurs Reug-Reug et Siteu, il s'était prêté à quelques démonstrations de lutte sénégalaise, sous les acclamations d'un public enthousiaste. Sa visite s'était poursuivie au Monument de la Renaissance africaine, où une démonstration de danse traditionnelle « Kumpo », issue de la culture diola, lui avait été présentée. Sa venue coïncidait également avec les célébrations du deuxième sacre continental des Lions du Sénégal à la Coupe d'Afrique des nations (CAN) 2025. Le streamer avait ainsi pris part à l'effervescence populaire entourant le retour des champions d'Afrique, après leur victoire face au Maroc en finale. Cette tournée africaine, qui s'est achevée le 27 janvier 2026, aura permis à IShowSpeed de mettre en lumière différentes expressions culturelles du continent, des spécialités culinaires aux danses traditionnelles, en passant par les pratiques sportives. Son passage au Sénégal avait notamment contribué à exposer des lieux emblématiques du pays à une audience internationale. A.N

items.title: Sam Jonah calls on Mahama to restore Gen Acheampong’s military rank, says Ghana must correct injustice of 1979 execution
items.description: Business magnate and former AngloGold Ashanti Chairman, Sir Sam Jonah, has called on President John Mahama and the Ghana Armed Forces to restore the military rank of former Head of State, General Ignatius Kutu Acheampong, arguing that his execution in 1979 without trial should not permanently erase his military identity and years of service. Speaking at the second edition of the General Kutu Acheampong Public Lecture Series, Sir Sam Jonah said the former military ruler was stripped of his rank by decree before being executed by firing squad on June 16, 1979, without being convicted by any court. He argued that restoring Acheampong’s rank should not be interpreted as an endorsement of his administration or an attempt to erase the suffering of people who experienced his rule. Rather, he said, the appeal was rooted in the principles of due process and the need to correct what he considers an enduring historical injustice. “Due process is not a reward for the virtuous. It is a protection for all of us, and above all, for those who we have decided we even dislike,” he stated. Sir Sam Jonah noted that other former military leaders who were executed during the same period have retained their military titles in historical records, while Acheampong continues to be referred to as Mr Acheampong. He described the situation as an unhealed national wound and urged the President, the Armed Forces Council and Parliament, where applicable, to take steps to restore the former Head of State’s military identity. His proposals include restoring Acheampong’s rank of General, reinstating his name on the rolls of the Ghana Military Academy and returning to his family the honours associated with his rank. Sir Sam Jonah also referenced a 2019 acknowledgement by the Ghana Armed Forces that the executions carried out in 1979 were an aberration, arguing that the decision to strip Acheampong of his military rank should equally be reconsidered. Beyond the circumstances of his death, he urged Ghanaians to acknowledge some of the initiatives associated with Acheampong’s administration, including Operation Feed Yourself, which promoted domestic food production and agricultural self-sufficiency. He also highlighted policies relating to Ghanaian participation in the mining industry and the decision by Acheampong’s government to facilitate the return of Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah, from exile for burial in Ghana in 1972. For Sir Sam Jonah, restoring Acheampong’s rank would not amount to rewriting Ghana’s history but completing it. “As Ghana approaches 70 years of independence, I can’t think of no better proof that this republic is confident enough to tell its true whole story. Restoring a rank does not rewrite history. It completes it,” he said.

items.title: Panne mondiale d’Outlook : Microsoft annonce une reprise progressive
items.description: Microsoft a annoncé ce vendredi une amélioration progressive de ses services touchés depuis jeudi par une panne mondiale. Outlook, Teams et Copilot restent toutefois perturbés dans certaines régions, avec des difficultés d’accès intermittentes et des retards dans l’acheminement des courriels. Le géant américain fait état de « progrès continus » dans le rétablissement de ses services. Des améliorations ont notamment été constatées en Amérique du Nord et dans une grande partie de l’Europe, tandis que des signes jugés « encourageants » de reprise sont également observés dans la région Asie-Pacifique. Microsoft prévient néanmoins que le retour à la normale n’est pas encore complet. Certains utilisateurs peuvent toujours rencontrer des difficultés pour accéder aux services ou constater des retards dans la réception et l’envoi de leurs courriels. Les perturbations concernent notamment Outlook, la messagerie de Microsoft, mais également Teams et Copilot, l’assistant d’intelligence artificielle du groupe. Microsoft explique que l’incident est survenu dans un contexte de forte charge sur ses infrastructures. L’entreprise travaille désormais à stabiliser les systèmes concernés, à résorber les files d’attente et les retards d’e-mails et à vérifier la cohérence du fonctionnement des différents modes de connexion. « Nous sommes profondément désolés des perturbations que cet incident a causées à nos clients et partenaires » , a indiqué Microsoft, assurant prendre pleinement la responsabilité de la situation. Concernant l’origine de cette panne, Microsoft affirme ne disposer, à ce stade, d’aucun élément indiquant une activité malveillante. L’entreprise concentre donc ses efforts sur la stabilisation de l’infrastructure et la résorption des perturbations restantes. La panne a néanmoins pris une ampleur mondiale, affectant des utilisateurs dans de nombreux pays. items.title: Les lionceaux reçoivent le drapeau national
items.description: À quelques jours de leur départ pour le Qatar, les Lionceaux du Sénégal ont reçu, ce vendredi 13 novembre, le Drapeau national des mains de la ministre de la Jeunesse et des Sports, Djirèye Clotilde Coly. Une cérémonie qui marque le début de leur mission mondiale, avec l’ambition de faire honneur au football sénégalais. Les couleurs nationales sont désormais confiées aux Lionceaux. Au Stade Léopold Sédar Senghor, la ministre de la Jeunesse et des Sports, Djirèye Clotilde Coly, a procédé, ce vendredi 13 novembre 2026, à la remise officielle du Drapeau national à la sélection masculine U17. Celle-ci représentera le Sénégal à la Coupe du monde de la catégorie, prévue au Qatar du 19 novembre au 13 décembre 2026. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence de membres du bureau de la Fédération sénégalaise de football (FSF), notamment du secrétaire général et du troisième vice-président, Pape Sidy Lô. Prenant la parole au nom du président de la Fédération, ce dernier a souligné l’importance de cette participation, qui offre au Sénégal une nouvelle occasion de faire rayonner son football sur la scène internationale. Au nom des joueurs, le sélectionneur national, Lamine Sané, a réaffirmé la détermination du groupe à défendre dignement les couleurs nationales. Il a assuré que les jeunes joueurs donneront le meilleur d’eux-mêmes pour représenter le pays durant cette compétition mondiale. Dans son allocution, la ministre a, pour sa part, invité les Lionceaux à faire preuve de détermination, de discipline et d’esprit de conquête. Elle les a exhortés à poursuivre la dynamique des performances du football sénégalais, en rappelant notamment leur sacre continental décroché à Rabat, en juin 2026. Un parcours qu’elle les encourage à prolonger sur la scène mondiale. En remettant le Drapeau national au nom du président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye, Djirèye Clotilde Coly a rappelé aux jeunes internationaux la responsabilité qui leur incombe : porter haut les couleurs du Sénégal et se montrer dignes ambassadeurs de la Nation. « L’esprit du Lion, c’est le combat, c’est l’offensive, c’est le courage ! », a lancé la ministre aux joueurs. Un message de mobilisation à quelques jours du rendez-vous qatari, où les Lionceaux tenteront de faire honneur au football sénégalais et de porter les espoirs de tout un peuple. Pour rappel, la Coupe du Monde U-17 de la FIFA 2026 se déroulera au Qatar du 19 novembre au 13 décembre 2026 A.N

items.title: Bawumia pledges to make agriculture a national security priority
items.description: New Patriotic Party (NPP) flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia has pledged to make agriculture a national security priority if elected President, citing challenges facing rice farmers and the need to strengthen Ghana’s food security. Speaking to rice farmers at Asutsuare in the Shai-Osudoku District, Dr Bawumia said his proposed government would adopt a more deliberate approach to agricultural development, given the sector’s importance to national survival and economic stability. He identified difficulties accessing fertiliser, inadequate irrigation infrastructure and the lack of reliable markets for locally produced rice as some of the challenges requiring urgent attention. Some farmers who interacted with him said they had taken loans to expand production but were struggling to recover their investments because buyers were not purchasing their produce. Dr Bawumia said Ghana needed to move beyond promises and implement policies that would give farmers the support and market access required to increase production and earn sustainable incomes. He called for the completion of Phase Two of the Kpong Irrigation Scheme, saying improved irrigation infrastructure would help expand rice cultivation and strengthen domestic production. The NPP flagbearer also proposed that schools and other public institutions be supplied with locally produced rice to provide farmers with a more reliable market. He argued that such an arrangement could help absorb local production, improve farmers’ incomes and reduce the country’s dependence on imported rice. His proposals come amid concerns about unsold stocks of locally produced rice and Ghana’s continued reliance on imports, despite efforts to expand domestic production. Dr Bawumia maintained that treating agriculture as a strategic national priority was necessary to strengthen food security and improve the livelihoods of farmers.

items.title: Ziguinchor veut miser sur le sport pour briser les barrières du handicap
items.description: Dans la capitale régionale du Sud, le handicap ne doit plus être un obstacle à la pratique sportive ni à la participation à la vie sociale. À travers un projet de deux ans, l’ONG Aïda mise sur le handisport pour renforcer les capacités des personnes en situation de handicap et faire du sport un véritable levier d’autonomie et d’inclusion. ZIGUINCHOR – Sur un fauteuil roulant, ils vont bientôt avoir le ballon entre les mains et le regard tourné vers le panier. C’est ce défi que les personnes en situation de handicap s’apprêtent à relever un nouveau défi. Ici, on veut faire du sport un espace où chacun peut trouver sa place, développer ses capacités et prendre part à la vie collective. À Ziguinchor, cette ambition prend forme avec le lancement, hier, d’un projet consacré à la promotion de l’inclusion sociale et économique des personnes handicapées par la pratique sportive. Mis en œuvre par l’ONG Aïda, avec le financement de la coopération valencienne et l’appui du ministère de la Famille, de l’Action sociale et des Solidarités, à travers la Direction régionale de l’Action (Dras), ce programme s’étend sur deux ans. Il entend favoriser l’accès des personnes en situation de handicap aux activités sportives, tout en formant des ressources humaines capables de pérenniser cette dynamique dans la région. Pour amorcer cette démarche, une formation de dix jours, prévue du 12 au 22 novembre, est organisée au profit des athlètes et des encadreurs. Elle porte principalement sur le basket-ball en fauteuil roulant, mais prévoit d’autres disciplines, notamment le volley-ball. Cette approche repose sur un principe de formation. « Nous lançons un projet sportif entièrement destiné aux personnes en situation de handicap, avec pour objectif de favoriser leur inclusion sociale et économique dans la région de Ziguinchor », a expliqué Blanca Orduna, coordonnatrice de l’ONG Aïda. Des bénéficiaires appelés à devenir des encadreurs Les participants, une fois formés, vont devenir des encadreurs afin d’élargir le nombre de bénéficiaires. Au-delà de l’initiation à la pratique sportive, l’ambition est de former des ressources humaines capables, à leur tour, de transmettre leurs connaissances et d’encadrer d’autres personnes « handicapées ». « Nous voulons que toutes les personnes vivant avec un handicap puissent profiter de cette initiative. Chacun doit avoir la possibilité de maîtriser le basket-ball en fauteuil roulant et de prendre part aux activités proposées », a-t-elle souligné. Pour la Ligue handisport de Ziguinchor, cette initiative vient répondre à une attente des personnes concernées. Son président, Henry Ndecky, salue un accompagnement qui, selon lui, pourrait contribuer à donner un nouvel élan au sport adapté dans la région. « Nous accueillons avec beaucoup de satisfaction cette initiative de l’ONG Aïda, qui s’engage à accompagner le handisport pendant deux ans à Ziguinchor. Les efforts que nous consentons aujourd’hui porteront leurs fruits dans les années à venir », s’est-il réjoui. Au-delà de la dimension sportive, le responsable insiste sur la nécessité de garantir aux personnes « handicapées » les mêmes droits et les mêmes possibilités de participation que les autres citoyens. « Le sport est un droit pour tous. Les personnes en situation de handicap ne doivent pas être oubliées et les pouvoirs publics doivent davantage les prendre en compte », a plaidé M. Ndecky. À travers ce programme, l’ONG Aïda et la Ligue handisport entendent ainsi faire tomber les barrières qui limitent encore l’accès des personnes « handicapées » à la pratique sportive. À Ziguinchor, l’enjeu dépasse désormais les terrains. Et tous souhaitent faire du sport un instrument de dignité et de pleine participation à la vie de la communauté. Gaustin DIATTA (Correspondant)

items.title: CAN 2027, Algérie – Togo : à quelle heure et sur quelle chaîne ?
items.description: L’équipe d’Algérie reprend la compétition avec un match contre le Togo ce vendredi 14 novembre au stade Hocine Ait Ahmed de Tizi-Ouzou pour le compte de la 3 e journée des qualifications pour la Coupe d’Afrique des nations (CAN 2027). Voici les informations nécessaires pour suivre le match en direct. Après la première mitigée de l’ère Brahim Hemdani fin septembre dernier, avec une victoire contre la Zambie (3-1) et un match nul en déplacement contre le Burundi (2-2) , l’Algérie accueille le Togo vendredi à Tizi-Ouzou (20h00). L’enjeu est double. D’abord, gagner pour rester à la tête de son groupe et rassurer les supporters après l’incident qui a marqué le match contre la Zambie durant lequel le défenseur Rayan Ait Nouri a eu un accrochage verbal avec le staff technique des Fennecs, ce qui lui a valu l’expulsion du groupe. Cet épisode a été suivi d’un match nul face au Burundi (2-2) à Bujumbura où les Verts ont étalé, une nouvelle fois, leurs carences défensives. Algérie – Togo : les Fennecs privés de plusieurs joueurs pour blessures Pour le match de ce vendredi, la tâche des hommes de Hemdani ne sera pas facile en raison de l’absence de quelques joueurs clés pour blessures notamment l’attaquant Bachir Belloumi et le milieu de terrain Hicham Boudaoui qui a été remplacé par Adem Zorgane. Le gardien Abdellatif Ramdani a quitté le stage après le décès de son père dimanche dernier. Il a été remplacé par le portier de l’Olympique d’Akbou Rayane Yesli. L’équipe d’Algérie a perdu deux autres joueurs pour blessures. « Victime d’une blessure au mollet lors de la séance d’entraînement de mercredi soir, l’attaquant Amin Chiakha a effectué, ce jeudi, des examens médicaux qui ont confirmé une lésion musculaire. De son côté, Rafik Belghali, qui souffrait de douleurs persistantes au niveau du genou, a été contraint d’interrompre la séance d’entraînement. Les deux joueurs sont, par conséquent, forfaits pour la double confrontation face au Togo, comptant pour les éliminatoires de la CAN 2027 », a indiqué la Fédération algérienne de football, en précisant que Hemdani a décidé de « les libérer et de faire appel à Saâdi Radouani, sociétaire de l’USM Alger. » Pour ce match, l’équipe d’Algérie part avec un léger avantage. Sur six confrontations entre les deux sélections, les Fennecs ont gagné à trois reprises et perdu deux fois. items.title: A Reader’s Perspective on Federalism, Insecurity, and the Pursuit of an Own Ethnic Region in Southern Ethiopia
items.description: A book chapter by Beza Dessalegn entitled “Federalism, Insecurity, and the Pursuit of an Own Ethnic Region in Southern Ethiopia” in the book Ethiopia’s Insecurity Complex: Protest, Transition and War , published in 2025 examines the under researched direct relationship between federalism and security in Ethiopia. The chapter analyses the pre- and post-2018 quest for regional statehood and the securitized responses of the federal and regional governments to these demands. It situates its analysis within the framework of “emerging anarchy,” exploring the relationship between Ethiopia’s federal structure and security in the context of rising demands for autonomy. Given the book chapter addresses the historical-comparative political development of the pre-and post-2018 regional statehood claims and state response, and the national dialogue process that might rethink the whole state structure arrangement, the review would contribute to an ongoing discussion on federal structure, social cohesions and state building. Using the former Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples’ (SNNP) Region as a case study, the chapter argues that both the creation and disintegration of the region were driven by political competition among dominant ethnic groups, as well as the pursuit of identity, self-determination, and regional autonomy by constituent ethnic communities. The main argument of the chapter is that the federal system, which was supposed to advocate for ensuring self-rule, has been challenged by the rising demands for self-rule. This is further challenged by the inconsistent granting of regional status and the securitized responses of the federal and regional governments. These demands in turn came to be perceived as threats to regime security and the continuity of the federation as a whole. The government’s perception of such demands as threats to regime security and national unity was evident both before and after the 2018 political development. This perception is not an isolated scene rather it is grounded in the broken promises, historical grievances, and the longstanding historical relationship among groups and with the state. The book chapter also raise the fact that these demands are rooted in the historical relationship and power dynamics, manifesting as both horizontal and vertical insecurity. The chapter further claims the lack of institutional mechanisms that can sufficiently tackle differences without it leading to violence. However, the formation of the regional state appears to have excluded minorities within regions from political rights perpetuating erosion of societal cohesion. On the other hand, the chapter frames the role played by political elites in weaponising ethnicity to materialize displacements, without any accountability, within the layers of security threats and insecurity patterns. However, the book chapter gave less emphasis to the discussion of institutional responses especially in their lack of capacity, tokenistic approach and domino effect. The institutional response inadequacy can be attested by the Administrative Boundaries and Identity Issues Commission’s conclusion that the majority of residents preferred the continuity of the SNNP region despite the widespread violence, and reports of threats and calls for the expulsion of the region’s ethnic minorities from their regions. This can also be taken as a lesson for institutions/commission with defect in their nature or performance. Finally, the chapter is being reviewed amid the convening of the National Dialogue, which has proposed shifting the authorship of the FDRE constitution to “the people of multinational Ethiopia” and granting the federal government a broader mandate to intervene in regions experiencing conflicts presumed to constitute emergencies. This context adds another dimension to the chapter’s analysis: a legalized unsolicited federal intervention could produce unintended consequences for the balance between regional autonomy and state consolidation particularly if what constitutes “ internal conflict of an emergency nature ” is not clearly predefined. This is especially relevant to the chapter’s conclusion on the need for a proactive response, inclusive governance, and a human-centered approach. items.title: Human rights and Democratic futures: Reflections from West and Central Africa
items.description: The future of human rights in Africa will not be secured by defending yesterday’s institutions alone. It requires reimagining the relationship between rights, democracy, dignity, and the everyday aspirations of citizens. There is a fundamental question confronting the human rights movement in Africa today: How do we defend human rights in societies where many citizens increasingly question whether democracy, constitutionalism, and the institutions established to protect their rights are delivering meaningful improvements in their lives? This question is particularly urgent in West and Central Africa, where democratic aspirations coexist with military interventions, constitutional controversies, violent extremism, economic exclusion, and growing pressures on civic freedoms. Yet these same regions are also home to extraordinary traditions of civic resistance, community solidarity, constitutional activism, women’s leadership, and youth mobilisation. The recent convening on the future of human rights in West and Central Africa provides an important opportunity to reflect on these contradictions. Beyond the immediate challenges confronting human rights defenders, it invites us to interrogate the assumptions, approaches, and institutional arrangements that have shaped human rights work over the past three decades. Our central argument is that the future of human rights and the future of democracy in Africa are inseparable. But their relationship must be understood more expansively than the defence of elections, constitutions, and formal institutions. Human rights must become meaningful in the everyday experiences of citizens, while democracy must be judged not only by how leaders acquire power but also by how power is exercised, whose interests it serves, and whether it advances human dignity. It is a warning the Nigerian political economist Claude Ake issued a generation ago: a democracy reduced to periodic elections, he argued, risks becoming the democratisation of disempowerment; a ritual of voting that leaves intact the structures that keep people poor, insecure and voiceless. It is echoed in the Indian jurist Upendra Baxi’s insistence that the legitimacy of human rights is measured not by the elegance of our norms but by their capacity to answer human suffering. The crisis is not only democratic regression. It is also a crisis of relevance. Across West and Central Africa, the democratic transitions of the 1990s generated considerable optimism. Multiparty elections returned, constitutions were rewritten, civil society expanded, and regional institutions developed increasingly ambitious frameworks for democratic governance and human rights. These were important achievements. They created opportunities for participation, strengthened normative commitments, and established institutional foundations for challenging abuses of power. Yet political liberalisation did not consistently produce economic transformation, social inclusion, or responsive governance. For many citizens, the promise of democracy has remained distant from the realities of unemployment, insecurity, inadequate public services, corruption, and unequal access to opportunities. This disconnect has profound implications for human rights. Ake saw the danger clearly. Because the colonial and post-colonial state remained the principal route to wealth and security, he observed, the struggle to control it turned politics into a form of warfare; multiplying parties without transforming that state would produce elections everywhere and popular power nowhere. The legal scholar Amy Chua sounded a complementary alarm in World on Fire : exporting free markets and overnight elections together into deeply unequal societies, without redistribution or social protection, can convert economic grievance into communal resentment and make democratic politics the arena in which that resentment is organised. Both warnings have aged well in West and Central Africa, where liberalisation of the ballot and of the market arrived together, and where too many citizens experienced both as systems rigged for others. When rights are presented primarily as legal guarantees, procedural protections, or international obligations, without sufficient attention to the material conditions that make their enjoyment possible, they risk appearing disconnected from the daily struggles of ordinary people. A young person who can vote but cannot find dignified employment may question the value of political participation. A woman whose constitutional equality is guaranteed but whose economic opportunities and physical safety remain constrained experiences a democracy that is incomplete. A rural community living with persistent insecurity may struggle to reconcile the language of citizenship with the absence of effective state protection. These experiences do not diminish the importance of civil and political rights. Rather, they demonstrate why such rights must be understood alongside economic, social, cultural, and collective rights. The challenge is not to replace one category of rights with another but to recover their indivisibility. Baxi’s formulation remains the sharpest test available: the foundations of human rights lie not in abstract theories of human nature but in concrete histories of human suffering. Rights that do not answer suffering will not command allegiance. When the state becomes both protector and source of insecurity The relationship between citizens and the state is undergoing significant strain. In parts of the Sahel, military authorities have justified extraordinary restrictions on political participation and civic freedoms by invoking national security and sovereignty. Elsewhere, civilian governments have faced criticism over restrictions on dissent, disputed constitutional arrangements, and the conduct of security institutions. Meanwhile, violent extremist groups, armed movements, criminal networks, and other non-state actors continue to threaten communities and undermine the protection of civilians. These developments expose a central dilemma: the state is expected to guarantee human rights, yet its institutions may themselves contribute to violations, exclusion, or insecurity. This is not an argument for weakening the state. On the contrary, effective and legitimate public institutions remain essential to the protection of rights. But state authority cannot be treated as an end in itself. Its legitimacy must rest on accountability, public trust, and the protection of the people it exists to serve. Nor should the understandable demand for security become a justification for indefinitely suspending freedoms. These dilemmas have deep historical roots. Ranajit Guha, the founding historian of Subaltern Studies, described colonial power as dominance without hegemony: rule sustained by coercion rather than consent. Too many post-colonial states inherited that grammar of rule. Where the state’s default relationship with society is domination, security easily becomes a language of repression, and citizenship remains thin in practice. Partha Chatterjee, writing in the same tradition, adds that beyond the enclaves of formal civil society, most people encounter the state not as rights-bearing citizens but as populations to be managed — negotiating survival through brokers, customary authorities and informal arrangements in what he calls political society. Human rights practice that speaks only the language of courtrooms and constitutions will struggle to reach them. Security and human rights are not competing objectives. Sustainable security depends on justice, inclusion, institutional legitimacy, and meaningful relationships between communities and public authorities. Where governments respond to insecurity primarily through coercion, without addressing the grievances that sustain conflict, they risk reproducing the conditions that undermine their own legitimacy. The future of human rights therefore requires stronger engagement with the political economy of insecurity, the governance of security institutions, and the lived experiences of communities at the margins of state protection. Human rights cannot remain the language of institutions alone One of the most consequential questions for the human rights movement concerns who defines its priorities, speaks in its name, and determines its strategies. Africa has a rich history of struggles for dignity, justice, freedom, and collective self-determination. These struggles predate contemporary international human rights institutions and cannot be reduced to frameworks imported from elsewhere. From anti-colonial movements to campaigns against military rule, from women’s organising to community struggles over land and natural resources, African societies have continually articulated their own understandings of rights and justice. Yet human rights practice can become overly professionalised, urban-centred and donor-driven, with accountability flowing upwards to funders rather than outwards to communities. This is also a question of the movement’s own legitimacy and ownership. These approaches have achieved important results and remain necessary. But they are insufficient when disconnected from the communities whose rights they seek to protect. The question is not whether international human rights standards remain relevant. Their universality remains essential, particularly when governments invoke cultural relativism or sovereignty to evade accountability. Issa Shivji has been among the most unsparing critics of this drift. Human rights in Africa, he reminds us, were forged in popular struggles against slavery, colonialism and dictatorship; when the discourse is professionalised, projectised and donor-funded, it risks being converted from a weapon of the oppressed into an ideology administered over their heads; one fluent in the vocabulary of accountability yet silent about the political economy that produces violation. Shivji’s conclusion is not that rights are a foreign imposition to be discarded. It is that rights are never granted from above: they are won, defended and extended through the struggles of ordinary people, and a movement that loses contact with those struggles loses both its legitimacy and its power. Rather, the question is how universal principles can be grounded in African experiences, histories, social relationships, and aspirations without compromising their substance. This requires community-based organising, local accountability and a polycentric movement: many centres of initiative, united by shared principles rather than a single institutional voice. It also requires recognising communities as political actors and rights holders, not merely beneficiaries of programmes designed elsewhere. Gayatri Spivak’s celebrated question; can the subaltern speak poses the movement’s hardest test: whether those who claim to represent the marginalised end up effacing their voices in the very act of representation. The answer cannot be to speak on behalf of communities. It must be to build the conditions in which communities speak, organise and lead for themselves. A new generation is expanding the meaning of rights Across Africa, younger generations are increasingly challenging conventional boundaries between political rights, economic justice, and democratic participation. Their demands frequently connect accountability to employment, corruption to public services, policing to dignity, and political exclusion to broader questions of generational justice. Digital technologies have expanded opportunities for mobilisation, documentation, solidarity, and public scrutiny. They have also introduced new risks involving surveillance, disinformation, online harassment, and restrictions on digital freedoms. What is particularly significant is that many young people are not necessarily rejecting democracy. They are questioning forms of democracy that appear unable or unwilling to respond to their aspirations. This distinction matters and the response cannot simply be to persuade young Africans to appreciate existing democratic institutions. It must also involve making those institutions more responsive, inclusive, and accountable. What is emerging, in Baxi’s terms, is a shift from the politics of human rights; the management of standards by professionals and institutions towards a politics for human rights: insurgent movements in which those who suffer become the authors of the norms meant to protect them. Guha would have recognised in these mobilisations what he called the autonomous domain of popular politics: forms of organisation, solidarity and imagination that do not wait for elite permission. The task of the established movement is not to tutor this energy but to join it, resource it and defend its space. Human rights organisations should engage younger generations not as programme participants alone but as co-creators and leaders, while confronting their own internal hierarchies and exclusions. The same principle applies to women, persons with disabilities, displaced populations, informal workers, and communities historically excluded from decision-making. A democratic future cannot be built through the continued marginalisation of those who constitute its social foundation. Reclaiming African agency without abandoning universal principles The changing international environment introduces another dimension to this debate. Geopolitical competition, shifting development priorities, declining confidence in multilateral institutions, and accusations of selective application of international norms have complicated the operating environment for human rights organisations. Criticism of double standards in the international system deserves serious engagement. The credibility of human rights principles is weakened when violations are condemned in some contexts but minimised or overlooked in others. However, the response to inconsistency cannot be the abandonment of universal standards. Shivji’s own position is instructive here. The sharpest African critic of human rights as an ideology of empire has never doubted the universality of the demand for dignity; he questions only who is entitled to define it, deploy it and speak in its name. Universality is not weakened when it is claimed from below. It is authenticated. African agency should not be confused with the unrestricted authority of governments to determine which rights their citizens may enjoy. Sovereignty belongs ultimately to people, not merely to those who exercise state power. An authentically African approach to human rights must therefore combine historical consciousness, cultural legitimacy, and regional ownership with firm commitments to accountability, equality, and freedom. Ake insisted likewise that an African democracy worthy of the name could not be an abstract template indifferent to time and place; it had to be concrete, anchored in how people actually live, labour, organise and resist. The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights provides an important foundation. Its recognition of individual rights, peoples’ rights, duties, and collective wellbeing offers opportunities to reconnect human rights with questions of solidarity, development, participation, and social justice. Institutions such as the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights, ECOWAS, and relevant Central African regional mechanisms can play important roles. But their effectiveness depends not only on normative mandates. It also depends on political commitment, institutional independence, access to justice, implementation and solidarity across borders, including across linguistic divides. Regional human rights protection must become more accessible and consequential for the people it is intended to serve. From defending democracy to making democracy worth believing in For too long, democracy and human rights have sometimes been approached as separate fields of intervention. Democracy practitioners focus on elections, political participation, institutional reform, and constitutional governance. Human rights actors concentrate on freedoms, legal protections, accountability, and remedies for violations. In practice, these agendas are deeply interconnected. An election cannot be meaningfully democratic where citizens cannot freely organise, speak, associate, or challenge those in authority. Similarly, human rights protections remain vulnerable where political institutions lack accountability, checks and balances are weakened, and citizens have limited opportunities to influence public decisions. But the relationship extends beyond institutional safeguards. A democracy that protects freedom of expression while tolerating systematic economic exclusion remains incomplete. A government that promises economic development while suppressing political freedoms cannot claim to have resolved the question of human dignity. The future therefore lies in bringing together democratic governance, human rights, economic justice, and social inclusion as mutually reinforcing dimensions of public life. This means moving beyond an overwhelmingly defensive posture. Defending civic space, protecting activists, challenging unlawful detention, and resisting constitutional manipulation remain indispensable. Yet the human rights movement must also articulate a positive vision of the societies it seeks to help build. What does a rights-respecting economy look like? How should public resources be governed to advance dignity and equality? How can communities exercise meaningful influence over decisions affecting their livelihoods? What would democratic accountability mean for young people confronting unemployment, or for women whose unpaid labour sustains households and communities? These are not peripheral development questions. They are central questions about the future of rights. Ake’s answer was what he called social democracy: a democracy anchored in the material life of ordinary people, in which participation means real power over the decisions that shape livelihoods, and development is undertaken by the people and not merely for them. Chua’s analysis points to the same conclusion from another direction: a democracy that coexists with entrenched economic exclusion will eventually be consumed by the backlash it breeds. Democratic security and distributive justice stand or fall together. Reimagining the movement and its methods If the human rights movement is to remain relevant and effective, several shifts deserve consideration. First, it must reconnect rights advocacy with the lived realities of communities, recognising that dignity is experienced through both freedom and material wellbeing. It must learn to work where Chatterjee’s political society lives in informal settlements, markets, farms, transport networks and community associations, where most people actually negotiate with power and not only in the formal civil society of registered organisations and legal claims. Second, it must build alliances across institutional boundaries, linking rights defenders with labour, women’s and youth movements, environmental advocates and community groups, while engaging non-state power, including corporations and armed actors. Third, it must invest in intergenerational leadership and the sustainability of civic movements. A movement cannot continually speak about the future while reproducing structures that limit the participation and leadership of younger generations. Fourth, it must rethink the relationship between formal institutions and informal systems of accountability. Community dialogue, mediation, customary institutions, and local solidarity networks can contribute to rights protection when they operate consistently with equality, inclusion, and fundamental freedoms. Finally, philanthropy and development partners must examine their own approaches. Short funding cycles, fragmented interventions and donor-defined indicators can undermine movement autonomy; flexible support must combine rapid protection with long-term organising. Supporting the future of human rights requires patient investment in relationships, ideas, collective agency and the movement’s capacity to learn and assess its actual effects on people’s lives. It also requires the humility to recognise that durable transformation cannot be engineered through projects alone. It requires, above all, what Baxi calls taking human suffering seriously: measuring the movement’s work not by reports produced or funds disbursed, but by the difference it makes to those who bear the weight of violation. The future is not predetermined It would be a mistake to interpret the challenges facing human rights and democracy in West and Central Africa as evidence of an inevitable democratic decline. The region’s political trajectories are neither uniform nor predetermined. There are important examples of constitutional resilience, peaceful political transitions, civic mobilisation, institutional innovation, and communities organising to defend their rights. These experiences remind us that democratic progress is rarely linear. It advances through contestation, negotiation, setbacks, and renewed collective action. The task is therefore neither to romanticise the past nor to surrender to pessimism about the future. It is to learn from the limitations of previous approaches while building on the achievements that remain worth protecting. The convening on the future of human rights offers an opportunity to move this conversation beyond familiar diagnoses of shrinking civic space and democratic regression. The more consequential question is what kind of human rights movement, democratic institutions, and relationships between citizens and power will be necessary for the decades ahead. Our answer begins with a simple proposition: human rights must be reclaimed as the everyday language of dignity, justice, belonging, and collective possibility. For West and Central Africa, this means protecting fundamental freedoms while confronting economic exclusion; defending constitutionalism while demanding accountable governance; strengthening regional institutions while investing in community agency; and upholding universal principles while recognising African histories and aspirations. Baxi has described human rights as a politics of hope; a language through which people who suffer imagine, and insist upon, a different world. That is the register in which the African human rights movement must now speak. The future of human rights will not be determined solely in courtrooms, conference halls, regional institutions, or international forums. It will also be shaped in communities confronting insecurity, among young people demanding opportunity, through women’s struggles for equality, and wherever citizens insist that power must serve human dignity. The challenge before us is not simply to preserve the human rights architecture we have inherited. It is to make human rights and democracy sufficiently meaningful, inclusive, and transformative that future generations will see them not as distant promises, but as foundations of the societies they aspire to build. Guha called this the small voice of history: the persistent, often unrecorded insistence of ordinary people on their own dignity. The human rights architecture of the future will stand only if it is built around that voice; not speaking for it, not administering it, but amplifying it until power has no choice but to listen.

items.title: Rebuilding a World That Never Existed
items.description: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. When it comes to reading, I’m not a glutton for punishment—I didn’t get very far into Finnegans Wake —but I am drawn to interesting challenges. Among the most memorably difficult reads I’ve taken on was the 1926 book A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle . A cerebral but darkly funny epic poem whose plot is well summarized by its title, it is written in “synthetic Scots,” a language cobbled together from Scottish dialects by its author, Hugh MacDiarmid. (Although Scots survives as a minority language with many regional variations, none of them closely resemble MacDiarmid’s concoction.) I loved the verse for its woozy lyricism and nerded out on the text’s annotations; I was also fascinated by the author’s grand ambitions. MacDiarmid was part of a cultural movement known as the Scottish Renaissance, whose writers sought to revive the once-independent nation’s dialects and traditions. But did he really think he could kick off a national resurgence by inventing a language no reader could easily understand? And what would drive a writer to even try? This week, the Atlantic staff writer Lily Meyer explored a similar question in her article about What Remains , a novel written by Brais Lamela in Galician. First, here are six new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: The one source Bob Woodward can’t get to talk How to be an ethical Russophile The worst thing about AI writing “Memories of the Train,” a short story by Siqi Liu AI is destroying the trust between writers and readers. “Poem for the WaterShed,” a poem by Gretel Ehrlich Meyer calls Lamela’s choice to write in a language primarily spoken in a single region in the northwest of Spain “an artistic expression of commitment to his particular roots,” and it is—but Lamela also understands the futility of trying to re-create the past. The novel’s narrator is writing a thesis about a widow in Galicia, who resisted the dictator Francisco Franco’s effort to subjugate the area (the government flooded rural villages and banned the Galician language). Yet the narrator’s academic ambitions are as nostalgic as they are political. Feeling rootless and isolated in New York, he hopes, Meyer writes, “to create a home of some sort for the unsettled parts of himself.” Other authors in minority languages have been vocal about their motivations. Writers in Greenlandic, Basque, Welsh, and the Judeo-Spanish language of Ladino have eschewed dominant languages such as Spanish or English to preserve cultures that have been subsumed by larger nations. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o forsook English to write in Kikuyu, publicly rebelling against England’s rule in Kenya and explaining that he wanted to “reconnect to the patriotic traditions” of a “literature rooted among the people.” MacDiarmid, too, saw himself as resisting the English and their language; he hated them so much that he once wrote, in private correspondence, that he might prefer a Nazi victory over England. But unlike Ngũgĩ, who wrote in a language spoken by millions, the Scot was trying to build a lexicon that had never really existed. In this sense he is not unlike Lamela’s narrator, a person who finds “re-creation” to be, Meyer writes, “a source of stability as much as it is an escape.” Characters like this, Meyer adds, “aspire to inhabit history so fully that they might create a home, or at least a moment of rest and acknowledgment, for its unsettled ghosts.” Such attempts might be doomed to fail, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t noble, or even beautiful. MacDiarmid didn’t exactly rebuild Scottish literature, but he made a modernist work of art that I’ll never forget. Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic A Novel About Obsessively Digging Into the Past By Lily Meyer A new book by the Galician writer Brais Lamela chronicles the drive that many have to touch history, no matter how elusive it is. Read the full article. What to Read Dirtbag, Massachusetts , by Isaac Fitzgerald Though his memoir-in-essays is subtitled A Confessional , and though it opens by revising the story he and his family used to tell about his childhood, Fitzgerald doesn’t immediately lay bare the lingering pain of his tumultuous upbringing. The first 11 essays are plenty vulnerable: Fitzgerald writes that he was born of an affair; spent his early years living in a homeless shelter and then in low-income housing run by the Catholic Worker movement; moved to north-central Massachusetts, where “violence was the solution, problem, and consequence”; and began abusing alcohol and drugs before age 13. But these are mere “flashes of the past,” as Fitzgerald writes in the last essay, “My Story,” where he takes full control of the narrative of his life. As he admits to having avoided the full truth, Fitzgerald becomes his own confessor, the one with the power to forgive. — Kristen Martin From our list: Six books you should read twice Out Next Week 📚 On the Calculation of Volume (Book V) , by Solvej Balle 📚 The Imperfect City , by Paul Goldberger 📚 Love the Revolution , by Aleksandr I. Solzhenitsyn Your Weekend Read Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic Zelda ’s Midlife Crisis By Ian Bogost This idea, that a video game could facilitate exploration in a simulated world bigger than the challenges choreographed inside it, is now so familiar that it counts as cliché. But at the time, it was startling. Popular culture—even Star Wars —was not yet understood by its consumers as world building, a now-popular name for constructing a fictional universe and then situating characters and stories inside it. Tolkien had been popular for decades, of course, but high fantasy was still largely considered escapist and—apologies—somewhat cringeworthy. To obsess about a false world real enough to imagine occupying remained strange, a fixation of dweebs unable or unwilling to live in the real one. Read the full article. items.title: La FTAV et l’IATA signent une convention pour faciliter l’accès au système d’accréditation GoLite
items.description: La Fédération Tunisienne des Agences de Voyages et de Tourisme (FTAV) a le plaisir d’annoncer la signature, le 12 Novembre 2026, au siège de la Fédération, d’une convention de partenariat avec l’Association du transport aérien international (IATA) représentée par son directeur régional pour l’Afrique du Nord Monsieur Mohamed Kadrouch. Fondée en 1945, l’Association du transport aérien international (IATA) représente, en 2026, plus de 370 compagnies aériennes, parmi lesquelles figurent les principaux transporteurs aériens mondiaux, issus de plus de 120 pays. Les compagnies aériennes membres de l’IATA assurent environ 85 % du trafic aérien mondial. L’IATA accompagne les activités des compagnies aériennes et contribue à l’élaboration des politiques et des normes régissant l’industrie du transport aérien. Son siège est établi à Montréal, au Canada. À travers cette convention, la Tunisie devient le 5ᵉ pays à l’échelle mondiale à bénéficier de cet accord, visant à faciliter l’accès des agences de voyages à l’accréditation IATA et à simplifier les démarches d’obtention de l’agrément GoLite. La FTAV poursuit son engagement pour accompagner ses adhérents et faciliter leur accès aux opportunités du secteur aérien. Communiqué L’article La FTAV et l'IATA signent une convention pour faciliter l’accès au système d’accréditation GoLite est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: RDC: au moins 44 morts civils tués dans de nouvelles attaques des ADF dans le nord-est du pays
items.description: Africa CDC, le Centre africain de contrôle et de prévention des maladies rattaché à l’Union africaine, a fermement condamné l’attaque meurtrière contre des civils à Cantine, en territoire de Beni, au Nord-Kivu, dans la nuit du 5 au 6 novembre. Une attaque dans une zone où sévit l’épidémie d’Ebola et qui a été attribuée au mouvement jihadiste ADF, qui a prêté allégeance à l’organisation État islamique. Et depuis, les incursions se poursuivent notamment dans le territoire voisin de Mambasa qui se trouve dans la province d’Ituri. Au moins 44 personnes ont été tuées entre le 9 et le 12 novembre. Le cumul de ces attaques des ADF amène à un bilan lourd d'au moins 110 personnes tuées en une semaine par le groupe armé dans la région en proie à Ebola.
